In 2018, a helicopter pilot flying over the mountains of British Columbia noticed an astonishing sight: a vast hole in the snow, with a river plunging into its depths.

The opening lies in Wells Gray Provincial Park, stretching roughly 330 feet long and 200 feet across at the rim. A climber descended about 260 feet down its sheer walls, but the waterfall’s powerful roar kept him from going farther. Laser scans mapped the slope to at least 443 feet without finding the bottom. Mist from the falls hides what lies below, so the pit’s true depth remains unknown.

Locals call it “Sarlacc’s Pit,” after the Star Wars creature. Aerial photos from as far back as 1949 show the site blanketed in snow—even in summer—suggesting the opening may have formed relatively recently. Scientists suspect the river resurfaces at a spring more than a mile away, but its underground route has yet to be confirmed. The area is now closed to visitors for safety reasons.

Make no mistake, this is about prosecuting the press, and this isn’t the first time something like
this has happened to me.
In New Orleans, LA, they falsely accused me of a felony and later admitted there was no felony.
The U.S. attorneys involved in that case were eventually disbarred.
The federal prosecutor was so furious about this case that he literally threw my book at me.

And the thing about me is – I never settle.
Most people find lawsuits stressful. The process becomes a form of punishment, but not to me.
I actually love this process.

⭐️ BlackRock wants tokenized funds to back traditional Wall Street trades 

📣 BlackRock has identified the use of tokenized investment funds as trading collateral in traditional financial markets as a potential next application for blockchain technology, building on existing arrangements that already allow institutional crypto traders to pledge tokenized fund holdings. Dan Maley, BlackRock’s head of cash management for Asia Pacific, said the firm’s tokenized funds are already being used as collateral in digital-asset markets. Extending that capability into conventional financial markets remains more complicated, although the asset manager sees opportunities for investors to transfer fund holdings without first redeeming them for cash.

🔔 The development moves BlackRock’s discussion beyond issuing digital representations of traditional investment products. Its focus now includes how those assets could function within the systems financial institutions use to settle transactions, secure trading positions and manage available cash. Collateral plays an established role in financial markets because banks, brokers and clearing firms require assets to secure loans, derivatives positions and other transactions. Investors commonly provide cash or eligible securities, with each receiving institution setting rules for the assets it will accept.

🔗 BlackRock sees a potential role for tokenized money market fund shares in that process. A tokenized share represents an interest in an investment fund while allowing certain transactions involving that interest to take place through blockchain infrastructure. In the Bloomberg interview, Maley described the opportunity to bring tokenized funds into the traditional financial ecosystem. He distinguished the collateral arrangements already operating in cryptocurrency markets from the more difficult work of connecting blockchain-based assets with established financial systems.

📡 Iran seeks regional partnerships to bolster food security: Deputy foreign minister

📌 Tehran, IRNA — Iran is ready to expand scientific, trade, and investment cooperation in agriculture with countries in the region and beyond, Deputy Foreign Minister for Legal and International Affairs Kazem Gharibabadi says, describing agricultural diplomacy as a means of securing sustainable food supplies.

Speaking at a World Food Day conference on Monday, Gharibabadi said food security required access to sufficient, safe and affordable food. Geopolitical crises, wars, climate change, drought, resource constraints and supply-chain disruptions were threatening millions of people.
​
Agriculture, he said, was not merely an economic sector but a pillar of national security, independence, development and stability. Cooperation in the field could build trust, strengthen international relations and ease tensions.
​
Gharibabadi said Iran's climate diversity, skilled workforce and research institutions offered a basis for partnerships.
​
He cited technology transfer, joint research, investment in agricultural infrastructure, efficient water use and sustainable supply chains as priority areas. Regional cooperation is needed to tackle water shortages, drought and dust storms through better water management, low-water farming methods, knowledge-sharing and early-warning systems.
​
Gharibabadi warned that wars and unilateral sanctions disrupt production and trade, saying that food, water and medicine must not become political tools.
​
He added that Iran was ready to cooperate with interested countries and international organizations, including the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), to promote food security. He also said damage to agricultural infrastructure during the 12-day and 40-day wars had not prevented Iran from maintaining food security.

Crypto Idea

Markets are facing a pretty ugly combination right now.

Brent crude is already nearing $113. Tensions around Iran are rising again, and the market is starting to price in the risk of another escalation. Meanwhile, the Nasdaq continues to slide, investors are getting increasingly nervous about the cost of the AI boom, and Bitcoin is heading lower again alongside other risk assets.

And here’s one simple thing that’s important to understand. Almost everything in the global economy ultimately comes down to energy. More expensive oil means higher transportation costs, higher production costs, and more expensive goods and services. If oil stays above $110 for an extended period, it will give inflation another boost.

From there, a familiar chain reaction kicks in. Inflation rises, the Fed has a harder time cutting rates, borrowing costs stay high, and pressure on stocks and crypto intensifies. That’s exactly why the current rise in oil prices matters much more to the market than it might seem at first glance.

There’s another risk on the horizon: November 3, when the U.S. midterm elections take place. Reports are already emerging that another round of strikes on Iran could be under discussion specifically after the elections. That doesn’t mean the war will necessarily escalate. But after November 3, the political constraints on the White House could genuinely change, and the market is already starting to factor that in.

For us, the priority right now isn’t trying to call the bottom, but watching oil as one of the key risk indicators. As long as Brent stays above $110, any positive news for stocks or crypto could quickly be overshadowed by inflation concerns and high interest rates. On the other hand, a sustained decline in oil prices could be the first sign that pressure on the markets is starting to ease.
